title: Shesha's hoods over the river
hook: the guards fall asleep, the bolted doors swing open, and Vasudeva walks out into the rain carrying a newborn
carry: seva: serving the Lord in every form
tomorrow: who is waiting on the other side of the river?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birth itself: four arms at midnight, and then, at Devaki's request, an ordinary baby. Your line was vatsalya: loving God as your own child.

The baby has only just been born, and he cannot stay. Kamsa's guards are just outside. Prompted by the Lord himself, the Bhagavata says, Vasudeva picks up his son, and the prison starts to come undone. The guards slump into sleep. The doors, bolted and barred with iron, open on their own, the way darkness gives way to the sun. Outside, rain is falling and the clouds rumble low. Somewhere ahead, in the dark, is the river.
screen: `A NEWBORN SON.` → `THE GUARDS SLEEP.` → `THE DOORS OPEN BY THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Notice who does what. The miracles open the way, but they don't carry the child. Vasudeva does that, in his own arms, at night, in the rain. Then the Bhagavata adds Shesha. The great serpent on whom Vishnu rests follows behind Vasudeva and spreads his hoods over father and child like an umbrella. Think about who Shesha is. In the ocean of milk, he is the Lord's bed. On this road, he's the Lord's umbrella. And the seventh child, drawn from Devaki's womb into Rohini's, Balarama, is a part of Shesha too, born to be the Lord's older brother; in many tellings of the Ramayana he came before as Lakshmana, Rama's brother. Bed, umbrella, brother: devotees read it this way, whatever the Lord needs, Shesha becomes. Hindus call that seva, service offered to God, and count it as worship in itself. It's why devotees are glad to sweep the temple floor, cook for a festival, or carry the deity in a procession. Then the river. The Yamuna is swollen and fast, full of waves and whirlpools, and it makes way, the text says, as the ocean once gave way for Rama on his road to Lanka. Later retellings add a basket on Vasudeva's head and the river rising to touch the child's feet; the Bhagavata's own account is shorter. A father, a child, a river giving way, and a serpent holding off the rain.
screen: `THE FATHER CARRIES THE CHILD` · `SHESHA SPREADS HIS HOODS` · `BED, UMBRELLA, BROTHER` · `SEVA: SERVICE OFFERED TO GOD` · `THE RIVER GIVES WAY`

segments.voice: Do one small piece of seva today, offered rather than noticed: wipe the shelf where your family prays, wash the pots after someone cooks, or set out fresh water or a flower. If you pray, offer it as you do it, the way Shesha holds his hoods over the Lord. If you don't, do it quietly for someone who won't find out it was you.
Shesha. The great serpent on whom Vishnu rests, who spreads his hoods over Vasudeva and the newborn child in the storm.

Seva: serving the Lord in every form, the way Shesha does. That's the week: prasad, the divine even in a dog, heaven that isn't the end, God coming down, then remembering him, loving him as a child, and serving. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The crossing of the Yamuna is retold at Janmashtami in songs, plays and temple tableaux, and Vasudeva carrying the infant under Shesha's hoods is a familiar image in Hindu art. Seva, service offered to God, is lived in temple and festival work: cleaning, cooking, serving food and carrying the deity in procession.
